analysis.one_liner: Reforms the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and adds DOE research, weatherization, and education programs for the Lower Mississippi Delta region.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill by voice vote on September 30, 1994, but the House never voted on it and it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would update how the government runs the Strategic Petroleum Reserve — the emergency oil stockpile — by removing outdated planning requirements and requiring emergency oil to be sold to the highest bidder. It also creates new Department of Energy programs in the poor Lower Mississippi Delta region: grants to weatherize low-income homes, energy-saving projects at schools and hospitals, scholarships at minority colleges, and a biomass energy research program. Finally, it opens DOE's national laboratories to closer research partnerships with private companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households in the Lower Mississippi Delta would gain weatherization grants and lower energy bills; schools and hospitals in the region would get conservation financing; students at minority colleges would gain scholarships. DOE national laboratories and private companies partnering with them would gain expanded authority to commercialize federally funded research, and oil companies would gain from simplified reserve rules and public competitive sales of emergency oil.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Delta-region families, minority colleges, DOE labs and industry partners

how_it_helps.text: Extends the federal weatherization program to low-income homes in the Lower Mississippi Delta, authorizing up to $20 million a year for FY1996-1998 [S3, S4].
Provides grants for energy conservation projects at Delta schools and hospitals, up to $2 million per recipient and $20 million per year [S4].

Creates scholarships and pre-college science programs at historically Black and minority colleges in the Delta Region, and requires annual reports on minority-college participation in DOE programs [S4].
Gives Hawaii binding offers and priority delivery schedules when buying oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, addressing that state's isolation from mainland supply chains [S4].

Streamlines Strategic Petroleum Reserve management, replacing dated planning mandates with modern drawdown, distribution, and reporting rules and extending the program's authority through FY 1999 [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the new grant programs, research demonstrations, and continued SPR operations through appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Title V directs federal laboratory funds toward cost-shared partnerships with industry, including a goal of committing at least 20 percent of multi-program lab research funds to industry partnerships, effectively subsidizing private R&D with public money [S4].

The bill repeals DOE-specific conflict of interest provisions and exempts national laboratory employees from certain post-employment restrictions, loosening ethics guardrails around the expanded industry partnerships [S4, S5].

It repeals the President's allocation authority and the requirement that SPR oil be sold under controlled distribution rules, replacing them with sales to the highest bidder — during a crisis, crude would go to whoever pays most, which may not be the regions or consumers most in need [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The parts aimed at ordinary people — weatherization, school and hospital conservation grants, scholarships — were modest and died with the bill. The parts that moved, like the technology-partnership title, direct federal laboratory resources toward private industry, with relaxed post-employment ethics rules for lab staff; taxpayers fund the research while private partners share the commercial upside. On balance the bill's largest public benefit would have been modest program support for a low-income region, and its largest structural effect was entrenching a publicly funded R&D pipeline into private hands.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the Senate by voice vote but was never scheduled for a House vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by voice vote on September 30, 1994 [S7].

The House received the bill on October 4, 1994, held it at the desk, and only referred it to the Agriculture Committee on November 29, 1994 — after the November elections — where it sat in subcommittee [S7].
No House vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1, S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing arrangements remained in place: DOE kept its older SPR statutory framework, and no Delta weatherization or education grants were created. DOE national laboratories did not gain the new partnership authorities, so industry did not gain those benefits either; the status quo won.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The congressional status quo; no Delta grants or lab authorities

for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment on August 12, 1994 [S7].

for.name: Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill by voice vote on September 30, 1994 [S7].

against.name: House of Representatives (103rd Congress)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill after Senate passage, held it at the desk, and referred it to committee and subcommittee without ever holding a vote before the Congress ended [S7].

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Referred the Senate-passed bill to its Subcommittee on Environment, Credit and Rural Development on November 30, 1994; no further action followed [S7].

sides.party_line_note: The Senate passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition or roll call, and no cosponsors are listed; the House never took a position [S6, S7].

industries.industry: National laboratory contractors and energy/manufacturing industry
industries.note: Title V opens DOE's national laboratories to industry partnerships, sets a 20% industry-partnership funding goal at major labs, waives cost-sharing for small businesses, and relaxes post-employment restrictions — public R&D capacity becomes more available to private firms [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Oil and gas refiners and marketers
industries.note: The bill modernizes Strategic Petroleum Reserve rules and mandates public competitive sales of emergency oil, which benefits bidders, while repealing allocation authority that once spread scarce oil by political allocation [S2, S4].

Louisiana State University and Southern University would anchor the Delta Energy Technology and Business Development Center, with federal grants and scholarship funding flowing to Delta institutions [S3, S4].
